rows.practice: puts problems into mathematical form, solves them with justified methods and draws valid inferences, reasoning logically from stated assumptions to conclusions
rows.knowledge: the core of calculus, linear algebra, probability and statistics, the basic language of the discipline and at least one programming language
rows.identity: a mathematical scientist in training who keeps to ethical standards, takes care with personal data and owns their learning through reflection and feedback

rows.practice: builds and tests models of real processes, programs and uses specialist statistical or optimisation software and synthesises methods across branches to attack unfamiliar problems from other disciplines
rows.knowledge: a range of areas of mathematics, statistics or operational research, how their results are derived and applied and the uncertainty that attaches to conclusions
rows.identity: a professional practitioner who works within legal and professional frameworks on data security, inclusion and sustainability and weighs the wider consequences of applied work

rows.practice: plans and carries out an advanced project, solving advanced problems in loosely defined settings and devising creative approaches to non-standard problems
rows.knowledge: a good command of the main body of the subject including advanced topics, with skill in building and judging rigorous logical arguments
rows.identity: an independent mathematical practitioner who knows their own strengths, recognises when to seek help and communicates arguments and uncertainty with confidence

tierReadings.note: No level 5 statements. Level 6 gives one academic standard and a set of professional standards with no typical or excellent split, so e2 draws on the professional standards in 4.9 and the modelling and computing content.

digest.definition: MSOR is treated as one body of knowledge and skill, wider than its three fields and often combined with others, as in data science
distinctiveFeatures: MSOR is treated as one body of knowledge and skill, wider than its three fields and often combined with others, as in data science
Mathematics draws conclusions by strict deduction from assumptions, and owes its reach to generalisation and abstraction
Statistics handles data under random variation on a base of probability, and explaining results to non-experts is central to it
Operational research spans heavily mathematical optimisation and rigorous non-mathematical problem structuring, in support of decisions
Courses run along a spectrum from theory-based to practice-based, each emphasis equally valued and read from the curriculum, not the title
The subject is cumulative, with strict prerequisites; accuracy with symbols and numbers matters; uneven attainment across modules is normal
It is widely taught to non-specialists as service teaching
Dense notation, board-based argument and diagrams shape both teaching and accessibility

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: the subject names its gender imbalance, awarding gaps and a curriculum centred on white Western men, and debates decolonising its history (eugenics, enslaved labour, fascist links) without cutting core content; inclusion also reaches data collection and analysis (D1, 1.21 to 1.27)

mathematical notation, board work, non-linear argument and diagrams defeat mainstream assistive technology, so the subject asks for specialist tools, trained support workers and staff support to embed accessibility (D1, 1.28 to 1.43)

headed Sustainability in the text: models for climate, epidemics, transport and health serve the UN goals; projects, modules and case studies carry it, along with the ethics of computing's footprint (D1, 1.44 to 1.48)
problem-solving is the core enterprise competency; projects, group work, data-heavy modules, client projects and placements build it, and graduates must be able to say how (D1, 1.49 to 1.60)

subjectSpecific.text: You should be able to bring together ideas and results from different branches of the subject.

transferable.text: You can expect to develop good study skills, above all the ability to learn on your own.
You can expect to become able to work on your own with patience and persistence, seeing a problem through to its end.
You can expect to learn to manage your work and deadlines efficiently.
You can expect to become adaptable, ready to take on new problems from areas you have not met before.
You can expect to learn to take what you know into new settings and to judge and tackle problems logically.
You can expect to become highly numerate and fully at ease with numbers and numerical arguments in everything you do.
You can expect to learn to use specialist software well and for the right jobs.
You can expect to develop IT skills and to find information from many sources, always citing them properly.
You can expect to learn to work with others and build on what they have done.
You can expect to learn to communicate in speech and in writing, presenting results clearly in reports, talks and posters.
You can expect to understand the ethical issues in your field, including care with personal data and the effects of applying mathematics.
You should be able to think critically and solve problems, both within the subject and in other fields where it is applied.
You should be able to work well on your own or as part of a group to reach a shared goal.
You should be able to communicate accurately and clearly, in speech and writing and in different formats, to specialists and non-specialists alike.
You should be confident with digital tools: finding information and checking whether it can be trusted, everyday IT, and choosing software that helps you think, reason and communicate mathematically.
You should be aware that your work has to fit professional and legal rules, including data security, equality, diversity and inclusion and sustainability, as they apply to mathematics.
You should keep to sound ethical standards and think about the wider effects of your work.
You should be able to start learning on your own and to check and adjust your plans as you reflect and receive feedback.

statements.paraphrase: Whatever the style of course, from theory-based to practice-based, providers should act so that every graduate can see themselves fully as a professional practitioner of the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Whether your course leans to theory or to practice, you should plan it so every graduate leaves able to identify fully as a professional practitioner in mathematics, statistics or operational research.

statements.about: EDI through curriculum, processes and monitoring
statements.paraphrase: Equality, diversity and inclusion should run through the curriculum and the whole learning experience; providers should examine curricula and processes, delivery, admissions and assessment among them, so no group is disadvantaged, and should monitor engagement and achievement by group and act on the results.

forPractitioner.text: You should build EDI into the curriculum and every part of the student experience, review delivery, admissions and assessment for their effects on particular groups, and monitor engagement and attainment by group so you can act for equity.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.paraphrase: Decolonising the curriculum is a live question for the subject; without dropping core content, provision might reflect the troubled settings some contributions came from and the gatekeeping around knowledge, and providers should review their practices with equity as the explicit focus, as 1.23 sets out.

forPractitioner.text: Keep core content, but reflect openly on the discipline's history, including contributions from contexts now seen as problematic and long-standing gatekeeping; you should review your practices with equity as the explicit focus.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.about: anticipatory accessibility and support for subject staff
statements.paraphrase: For an accessible course, providers should foresee what learners will need and meet it in advance, and institutions should help subject staff past the barriers peculiar to the subject, which can add much to the time spent making materials accessible.

forPractitioner.text: You should anticipate learners' needs and meet them before they are raised; your institution should give MSOR staff support (specialist staff, training, policy that allows for mathematical content, suitable tools) to overcome barriers the subject brings.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.about: barriers to participation at course and module level
statements.paraphrase: Providers should think through the barriers that stop students taking a full part in their education and academic communities, at course level and inside modules, so accessibility is handled coherently and consistently.

forPractitioner.text: You should consider the barriers to full participation both across the course and within each module, so the approach to accessibility is one coherent, consistent whole.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.about: embedding accessibility so adjustments are rarely needed
statements.paraphrase: It is essential that providers foresee disabled students' subject-specific digital, physical and teaching needs and build accessibility in, so that reasonable adjustments are needed as little as possible or not at all.

forPractitioner.text: It is essential that you anticipate the digital, physical and pedagogical accessibility needs disabled students have in this subject, and embed accessibility so individual adjustments are rarely or never needed.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.paraphrase: Providers should aim for well-curated courses, which help every student's mental health and lighten the administrative and cognitive load on disabled students, through clear communication of learning opportunities, well-spaced assessment and extra support when new ideas first appear.

forPractitioner.text: You should curate the course well: communicate learning opportunities clearly, space assessments sensibly and give particular support when a concept or skill first appears.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.about: extra resources where assistive technology fails
statements.paraphrase: Because mainstream assistive technology handles mathematical content poorly, providers should recognise the subject's particular needs and supply extra resources that mostly text-based subjects may not need.

forPractitioner.text: You should recognise that common assistive tools (screen readers, captioning, learning platforms) often fail on mathematical content, and fund the extra resources needed to close that gap.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.paraphrase: Online, hybrid or blended elements and captured sessions can widen access; suitable technology must be in place to capture live written work and caption it accurately, and in the room boards and displays must be visible.

forPractitioner.text: Where you capture or caption sessions, the technology must record extended written working and caption it accurately; in physical rooms, boards and displays must be visible to everyone.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.paraphrase: Scribes, notetakers, readers, communication support workers and others in support roles need to know the subject's terms and symbols, because a small change in a symbol can alter the meaning entirely.

forPractitioner.text: Those who support disabled students (scribes, notetakers, readers, communication support workers) need training in MSOR terminology and notation, since one wrong symbol can change what is meant.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.paraphrase: Assessment design should foresee and remove barriers unrelated to what is being measured, such as heavy interpretation of material, distracting images or unfamiliar context, customs or colloquial language.

forPractitioner.text: When designing assessments you should anticipate and strip out barriers that have nothing to do with the knowledge or skill measured: needless reading load, distracting imagery, unfamiliar cultural context or idiom.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.paraphrase: Helping students into work is an essential part of the degree; students own their career development and other services help, but employability skills should be built into the course, enterprise and entrepreneurship education included.

forPractitioner.text: Students carry personal responsibility for their careers and central services help, but you should embed employability skills in the course itself, through enterprise and entrepreneurship education among other means.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.paraphrase: Projects and dissertations build reflection, responsibility and supervised risk-taking, and group modules build influencing, leadership, negotiation and communication; before group work, students should be supported to understand how working with others differs from working alone and how good groups behave.

forPractitioner.text: Before any group task you should help students understand how collaborative work differs from individual work, how groups are managed and what good group behaviour looks like; projects, group modules and work with large data sets then build enterprise skills.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research degree

statements.paraphrase: To build on these skills later in work or study, graduates need to be able to reflect on, understand and explain how their degree let them develop enterprise, entrepreneurship and wider employability skills.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates need to be able to reflect on and explain how the course developed their enterprise and employability skills; give them chances to practise saying so.

forBeneficiary.text: To make the most of your skills in a job or further study, you need to be able to reflect on, understand and explain how your degree helped you develop enterprising and employability skills.

statements.about: what a bachelor's degree should give students
statements.paraphrase: Undergraduates may take a bachelor's degree with honours (FHEQ 6, FQHEIS 10) or an integrated master's with honours (FHEQ 7, FQHEIS 11), each with its own outcomes; bachelor's degrees should give students subject knowledge, understanding and skills and wider transferable skills that equip them for many careers.

forPractitioner.text: Your bachelor's course should equip students with the knowledge, understanding and skills of the subject and with transferable skills that open a wide range of careers; integrated master's courses carry their own higher outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: Bachelor's and integrated master's degrees may include study away from the institution, with credit set by the workload; where a placement carries credit it should be built into the programme so students can link the experience to their academic study.

forPractitioner.text: If a placement earns credit, you should integrate it into the programme so students connect what they did and learned there with their academic work.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: The academic part of an integrated degree apprenticeship in the subject should follow this statement's guidance; degree apprenticeships are described more fully in QAA's Characteristics Statement on apprenticeships.

forPractitioner.text: If you run an integrated degree apprenticeship in MSOR, its academic component should follow the guidance of this statement, read with the Characteristics Statement for apprenticeships.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: progression towards threshold; readiness for postgraduate study
statements.paraphrase: Students move up the levels of a bachelor's or integrated master's under their institution's rules; each level is expected to build towards reaching at least the threshold subject-specific and generic skills by the end, and a student with a second-class degree or better is expected to be ready for postgraduate study.

forPractitioner.text: Plan each level so it builds towards at least the threshold standards by the end; a graduate with a second-class degree or better is expected to be ready for postgraduate study, though each course sets its own entry rules.

forBeneficiary.text: As you move from one year to the next, each stage builds you towards at least the threshold level of subject and general skills by the end; with a second-class degree or better you can expect to be ready for postgraduate study, though each course sets its own entry rules.

statements.about: core skills of each subject in a combination
statements.paraphrase: Students on joint honours or interdisciplinary courses will reach the core of the specific and general skills of each subject they combine.

forPractitioner.text: Joint honours and interdisciplinary students will reach the core subject-specific and generic skills of each subject; make sure the MSOR half delivers its core.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study MSOR jointly with another subject, or on an interdisciplinary course, you will gain the core subject and general skills of each subject you combine.

statements.paraphrase: Students should have some freedom to choose optional modules that suit their interests, and suitable advice on those choices should be available.

forPractitioner.text: You should offer students some optional modules matched to their interests and give them proper guidance on choosing among them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: courses flexible to change and to learners
statements.paraphrase: Courses should be flexible enough to respond to, and anticipate, change in the subject, its links with other disciplines and the needs of graduates and employers, and should take account of learners' needs, making reasonable adjustments where required.

forPractitioner.text: You should keep the course flexible enough to anticipate and respond to change in the discipline, in neighbouring fields and in what graduates and employers need, and make reasonable adjustments for learners as required.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: Work with employers brings students many benefits and can shape the curriculum; where partners take part in delivering a degree, providers should set up oversight so the partners meet each relevant safeguard, quality standard and expectation.

forPractitioner.text: Where employers or other partners help deliver the degree (degree apprenticeships, for example), you should set up oversight so they meet the relevant safeguards, quality standards and expectations.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: Courses build subject-specific knowledge and skills; at higher levels these differ between graduates by what each pursued, and this variety, natural to the subject, is welcome and must not be limited at all, though a core shared by all graduates can be seen.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates' advanced subject knowledge and skills will differ with the areas they chose; you must not restrict that diversity, though all graduates still share an identifiable core.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a constraint on how courses and this statement are applied, not an outcome for the student

statements.about: numeracy, computing and modelling as general skills
statements.paraphrase: Courses will also produce graduates with well-developed general skills; plainly they should be highly numerate, and most will be competent with computing and modelling applications.

forPractitioner.text: Your graduates will have strong general skills: they should be highly numerate, and most will handle computing and modelling applications competently.

forBeneficiary.text: You will also develop strong general skills: you will be highly numerate and, like most of your peers, able to use computing and modelling with confidence.

headingPath: Areas of Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research

statements.about: knowledge of a range of areas
statements.paraphrase: Courses will give graduates knowledge of a range of areas of the subject, with understanding of how results are derived and applied that matches where the course sits between practice-based and theory-based.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will know a range of MSOR areas; the depth to which they understand derivations and applications will follow your course's place between theory and practice.

forBeneficiary.text: You will know a range of areas across mathematics, statistics and operational research, understanding how results are derived and applied to the depth your course's balance of theory and practice calls for.

headingPath: Areas of Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research

statements.paraphrase: Statistics courses give graduates core mathematics and several major statistical areas, such as inference, likelihood, linear modelling, time series, stochastic processes, exploratory work and analytics; graduates are able to analyse data with a statistical package.

forPractitioner.text: Statistics graduates will be able to analyse data with a statistical package, on a base of core mathematics and major statistical topics.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study statistics, you will be able to use a statistical software package to analyse data, building on core mathematics and major areas of statistics.

statements.paraphrase: Courses give graduates some knowledge of programming for computation; since computation and software are central to data analysis at work, graduates will be familiar with at least one programming language, will have used specialist software on the problems in hand and, where feasible, will know how its algorithms work.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will know at least one programming language and will have used specialist software on real problems; where you can, teach the algorithms behind it.

forBeneficiary.text: You will know at least one programming language, will have used specialist software on real problems and, where you can, will understand the algorithms behind it.

statements.paraphrase: Mathematical and statistical modelling represents processes abstractly; every graduate is expected to know and understand something of modelling, usually through problems from at least one application area.

forPractitioner.text: Every graduate is expected to have some knowledge and understanding of modelling, usually met through at least one application area; plan where the course teaches it.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to come away with some knowledge and understanding of mathematical and statistical modelling, usually through problems from at least one area of application.

statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: study skills, above all learning on one's own.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to have good study skills, especially independent learning; build these in from the start.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to develop good study skills, above all the ability to learn on your own.

statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: working alone with patience and persistence until a problem is solved.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to work on their own with patience and persistence, seeing problems through to the end.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to become able to work on your own with patience and persistence, seeing a problem through to its end.

statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: managing processes and deadlines efficiently.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to manage their processes and deadlines efficiently; give them practice with real schedules.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to learn to manage your work and deadlines efficiently.

statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: adaptability, especially readiness to take on new problems from unfamiliar areas.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to be adaptable, ready to tackle new problems from new areas.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to become adaptable, ready to take on new problems from areas you have not met before.

statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: carrying knowledge from one setting to another, judging problems logically and tackling them analytically.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to transfer knowledge between contexts and to assess and approach problems logically and analytically.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to learn to take what you know into new settings and to judge and tackle problems logically.

statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: highly developed numeracy, at ease with numerical ideas and arguments at every stage of work.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to be highly numerate and fully comfortable with numerical concepts and arguments throughout their work.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to become highly numerate and fully at ease with numbers and numerical arguments in everything you do.

statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: using specialist software appropriately.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to apply specialist software appropriately; give them practice choosing the right tool.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to learn to use specialist software well and for the right jobs.

statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: IT skills and finding information from varied sources, always citing them properly.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to have IT skills and to gather information from many sources, referencing each one properly.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to develop IT skills and to find information from many sources, always citing them properly.

statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: working with others and building on their work.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to collaborate and build on others' work.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to learn to work with others and build on what they have done.

statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: communication, verbal and non-verbal, and presenting results clearly in several forms such as reports, talks and posters.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to communicate verbally and non-verbally and to present results clearly in reports, presentations and posters.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to learn to communicate in speech and in writing, presenting results clearly in reports, talks and posters.

statements.about: ethical issues, personal data and impact
statements.paraphrase: Expected of all graduates: knowledge of ethical issues, including care with personal data and the effects of the subject when applied.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to know the ethical issues of the field, including sensitive handling of personal data and the impact of applying MSOR.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect to understand the ethical issues in your field, including care with personal data and the effects of applying mathematics.

statements.paraphrase: Teaching and learning methods vary with course style, content, the learners' level and route and the resources at hand; providers should choose carefully after weighing many pedagogies, expecting to mix approaches even within one module while keeping the student's experience coherent across the course.

forPractitioner.text: You should choose teaching approaches deliberately, after weighing a wide range of pedagogies; expect to combine several, even in one module, but keep the student's experience coherent from start to finish.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: peer learning and spaces for it
statements.paraphrase: Practice and repetition suit collaborative learning, and peer learning, in class or student-led, enriches each learner; providers should make formal and informal spaces available for group work and should promote peer learning in ways consistent with good academic practice, so students learn from others without compromising integrity.

forPractitioner.text: You should provide formal and informal spaces for group study and actively encourage peer learning, guided by good academic practice, so students learn from one another while keeping their work their own.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: Providers should accept that they share with students the responsibility for turning them into independent scholars and practitioners, which includes the scaffolding, confidence-building and opportunities students need to become effective independent learners.

forPractitioner.text: You should treat the growth of students into independent scholars as a responsibility you share with them, and supply the scaffolding, confidence-building and chances to practise that independent learning needs.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: equipping students to learn on their own
statements.paraphrase: Students need a large base of knowledge and practised skill before they can tackle harder problems alone, especially in abstract areas; providers should put first the discipline skills that let students learn the subject independently, recognising that this enriches the provision.

forPractitioner.text: You should give priority to equipping students with the discipline skills to learn MSOR content on their own, since much knowledge and practice must come before they can tackle advanced problems independently.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: study skills, scholarly habits and consolidation time
statements.paraphrase: Providers should help students build study skills; tutors should model and explain the worth of work outside timetabled hours, such as reading ahead, checking arguments and independent practice; scholarly habits like experimenting with ideas and attempting incomplete solutions should be encouraged; and teaching and assessment should be timed to leave room to consolidate.

forPractitioner.text: You should develop students' study skills, model the value of independent work outside class (reading ahead, checking proofs, practising problems and code), encourage exploratory scholarship and schedule teaching and assessment so students have time to consolidate.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: Computing runs through the subject, concentrated in modules or spread across a course; students develop computational thinking, should meet one programming language or more and may draw on specialist software such as computer algebra, numerical and statistical packages and optimisation software, beside spreadsheets, graphics and typesetting tools.

forPractitioner.text: Students should meet at least one programming language and develop computational thinking; decide whether computing sits in dedicated modules or runs through the course, and which specialist tools students use.

forBeneficiary.text: During your course you should meet at least one programming language and develop computational thinking, and you may use specialist software such as computer algebra, statistical packages or optimisation tools.

statements.paraphrase: Teaching keeps changing and innovation should be evaluated and shared; providers should support new staff to train in ways suited to the discipline and should ensure postgraduate tutors receive enough discipline-relevant training, and every member of staff carries a responsibility to keep developing professionally.

forPractitioner.text: You should give new MSOR staff discipline-appropriate training and make sure postgraduate tutors are properly trained for their role; every member of staff is responsible for their own continuing professional development.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: Providers should take part in quality assurance processes, local, statutory or tied to accreditation, to keep up and improve the quality of their provision.

forPractitioner.text: You should engage with quality assurance (your institution's own processes, statutory ones tied to degree awarding powers and those of accrediting bodies) to maintain and enhance provision.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: general characteristics as outcomes; EDI in assessment design
statements.paraphrase: The subject's general characteristics, such as precision with symbols, spatial awareness, pattern recognition, complex logical reasoning, proof and clear expression, can serve as intended outcomes of every course, and some assessments will test them; assessment design should take account of the equality, diversity and inclusion issues set out in 1.27.

forPractitioner.text: Treat the discipline's general characteristics (symbolic precision, spatial awareness, pattern-spotting, logical agility, proof and clarity) as outcomes some assessments test, and you should design assessment with the EDI points of 1.27 in mind.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: Assessment may use many methods suited to context and purpose, since learners show different aptitudes in different formats, with automatic online marking common for formative work; every assessment, invigilated examinations included, should be designed with accessibility and equality, diversity and inclusion in mind.

forPractitioner.text: Use a range of assessment methods, since students perform differently across formats; you should design every assessment, traditional exams included, with accessibility and EDI considered from the start.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: Annex D for performance above threshold; master's outcomes
statements.paraphrase: Most students will do much better than the minimum threshold; each provider decides how to evidence this and should refer to Annex D's descriptions of the four honours classifications; master's graduates build on the level 6 and 10 outcomes, in more depth in a specialist area, to the outcomes the Frameworks set for their level.

forPractitioner.text: To judge achievement above the threshold you should use Annex D of the Frameworks (the descriptions of first, upper second, lower second and third-class honours) with your own method of evidence; for master's awards use the Frameworks' level 7 and 11 outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in judging and evidencing achievement

statements.about: core body of knowledge and basic language
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show a reasonable grasp of the basic knowledge of the course, normally calculus, linear algebra and probability and statistics, and to follow the discipline's basic language.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should be able to show a reasonable understanding of the course's core knowledge (usually calculus, linear algebra and probability and statistics) and of the subject's basic language.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an honours degree, you should be able to show a reasonable understanding of the core of your course (usually calculus, linear algebra and probability and statistics) and follow the basic language of the subject.

statements.about: calculation, manipulation and solving set problems
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show reasonable skill at calculating and manipulating within that core, and some ability to solve problems set inside it.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should be able to show reasonable skill in calculation and manipulation within the core and some capability to solve problems framed in it.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an honours degree, you should be able to show reasonable skill at calculating and manipulating within that core knowledge, and some ability to solve problems set within it.

statements.about: applying concepts with justified choice of method
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show concepts and principles applied in well-defined settings, with judgement in choosing and using tools and techniques and a justification of the methods used.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should be able to apply concepts and principles in well-defined contexts, choose and use tools and techniques with judgement and justify their methods.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an honours degree, you should be able to show that you can apply ideas and principles in clearly defined situations, choose and use tools and techniques sensibly and explain why your method fits.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show reasoning by logical argument, naming the assumptions made and the conclusions reached.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should be able to reason through logical arguments, identifying the assumptions they rest on and the conclusions they reach.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an honours degree, you should be able to show that you can reason with logical arguments, saying which assumptions you made and what conclusions follow.

statements.about: formulating and solving problems; valid inferences
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show reasonable skill at understanding problems, putting them in mathematical form, solving them by suitable methods and drawing valid inferences.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should be able to show reasonable skill in understanding a problem, formulating it mathematically, solving it by suitable methods and drawing valid inferences.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an honours degree, you should be able to show reasonable skill at understanding a problem, writing it in mathematical form, solving it by a suitable method and drawing sound conclusions from the answer.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show logical arguments, evidence and conclusions communicated with reasonable accuracy and clarity, admitting the uncertainty of conclusions where fitting.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should be able to communicate arguments, evidence and conclusions reasonably accurately and clearly, acknowledging uncertainty in conclusions where relevant.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an honours degree, you should be able to show that you can explain arguments, evidence and conclusions reasonably accurately and clearly, saying how uncertain a conclusion is where that matters.

statements.about: a programming language and MSOR technology
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show they know one programming language or more and can use other suitable technology for the subject competently.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should be able to show they know one programming language or more and use other suitable MSOR technology competently.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an honours degree, you should be able to show that you know at least one programming language and can use other suitable mathematical software competently.

statements.appliesTo: graduates at the integrated master's threshold
statements.about: main body of knowledge with advanced topics
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show a good grasp of the main knowledge of the course, some advanced topics included.

forPractitioner.text: At the integrated master's threshold, graduates should be able to show a good understanding of the course's main body of knowledge, including some advanced topics.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an integrated master's degree, you should be able to show a good understanding of the main knowledge of your course, including some advanced topics.

statements.appliesTo: graduates at the integrated master's threshold
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show good skill at calculating and manipulating the material and the capacity to solve advanced problems framed within it.

forPractitioner.text: At the integrated master's threshold, graduates should be able to show good skill in calculation and manipulation and be capable of solving advanced problems in the material.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an integrated master's degree, you should be able to show good skill at calculating and manipulating the material, and that you can solve advanced problems set within it.

statements.appliesTo: graduates at the integrated master's threshold
statements.about: applying a range of concepts in loosely defined settings
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show a range of concepts and principles applied in loosely defined settings, with good judgement in choosing and using tools and techniques and a justification of the methods used.

forPractitioner.text: At the integrated master's threshold, graduates should be able to apply a range of concepts in loosely defined contexts, with good judgement in choosing tools and a justification of methods.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an integrated master's degree, you should be able to show that you can apply a range of ideas in loosely defined situations, choosing tools and techniques with good judgement and explaining why your methods fit.

statements.appliesTo: graduates at the integrated master's threshold
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show good capability in building and judging logical arguments.

forPractitioner.text: At the integrated master's threshold, graduates should be able to show good capability in developing and evaluating logical arguments.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an integrated master's degree, you should be able to show that you can build logical arguments of your own and judge other people's well.

statements.appliesTo: graduates at the integrated master's threshold
statements.about: formulating and solving problems; valid inferences
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show good skill at understanding problems, putting them in mathematical form, solving them by suitable methods and drawing valid inferences.

forPractitioner.text: At the integrated master's threshold, graduates should be able to show good skill in understanding, formulating and solving problems by suitable methods and drawing valid inferences.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an integrated master's degree, you should be able to show good skill at understanding a problem, writing it in mathematical form, solving it by a suitable method and drawing sound conclusions.

statements.appliesTo: graduates at the integrated master's threshold
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show confident, effective communication of logical arguments, evidence and conclusions, accurate and clear, admitting uncertainty where fitting.

forPractitioner.text: At the integrated master's threshold, graduates should be able to communicate arguments, evidence and conclusions confidently, accurately and clearly, acknowledging uncertainty where relevant.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an integrated master's degree, you should be able to show that you can explain arguments, evidence and conclusions with confidence, accuracy and clarity, saying how uncertain they are where that matters.

statements.appliesTo: graduates at the integrated master's threshold
statements.about: a programming language and MSOR technology
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show they know one programming language or more and can use other suitable technology for the subject competently.

forPractitioner.text: At the integrated master's threshold, graduates should be able to show they know one programming language or more and use other suitable MSOR technology competently.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an integrated master's degree, you should be able to show that you know at least one programming language and can use other suitable mathematical software competently.

statements.appliesTo: graduates at the integrated master's threshold
statements.about: independent work and knowing when to seek help
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show competent, independent working, awareness of one's own strengths and an understanding of when help is needed.

forPractitioner.text: At the integrated master's threshold, graduates should be able to work competently and independently, know their own strengths and recognise when they need help.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an integrated master's degree, you should be able to show that you can work competently on your own, know your strengths and recognise when you need to ask for help.

statements.appliesTo: graduates at the integrated master's threshold
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show competence in planning and carrying out an advanced project in mathematics, statistics, operational research or a related area.

forPractitioner.text: At the integrated master's threshold, graduates should be able to plan and carry out an advanced project competently, in one of the three fields or a neighbouring area.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an integrated master's degree, you should be able to show that you can plan and carry out an advanced project in mathematics, statistics, operational research or a related area.

statements.about: taught master's and the listed standards
statements.paraphrase: Taught postgraduate master's courses will build some or all of the standards above, depending on the course, which may specialise within one part of the subject or combine it with another discipline.

forPractitioner.text: A taught master's will develop some or all of the threshold standards in 4.5 and 4.6, depending on whether it specialises within MSOR or combines it with another discipline; state which apply.

forBeneficiary.text: On a taught master's course you will develop some or all of these standards, depending on whether your course specialises within the subject or combines it with another field.

statements.paraphrase: Graduates should be expected to bring together information from different branches of the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should be able to synthesise information drawn from different branches of MSOR; design tasks that cross module boundaries.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to bring together ideas and results from different branches of the subject.

statements.paraphrase: Graduates should be expected to use critical thinking and problem-solving on problems from within the subject and from other disciplines or applications.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should apply critical thinking and problem-solving to problems from MSOR and from other disciplines and applications.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to think critically and solve problems, both within the subject and in other fields where it is applied.

statements.about: working alone or in a group to an aim
statements.paraphrase: Graduates should be expected to work effectively alone or in a group towards a set aim.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should work effectively on their own or in a group to achieve a specific aim.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to work well on your own or as part of a group to reach a shared goal.

statements.about: communicating to specialist and non-specialist audiences
statements.paraphrase: Graduates should be expected to communicate accurately and clearly, verbally or non-verbally, in varied formats, possibly to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should communicate accurately and clearly, spoken and written, in a variety of formats, which may include specialist and non-specialist audiences.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to communicate accurately and clearly, in speech and writing and in different formats, to specialists and non-specialists alike.

statements.paraphrase: Graduates should be expected to have digital capabilities: finding information and judging its reliability, using general IT and choosing and using digital tools that support mathematical thinking, reasoning and communication.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should have digital capabilities: retrieving information and checking its reliability, general IT, and selecting digital tools to support mathematical reasoning and communication.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be confident with digital tools: finding information and checking whether it can be trusted, everyday IT, and choosing software that helps you think, reason and communicate mathematically.

statements.about: professional and legal frameworks, EDI and sustainability
statements.paraphrase: Graduates should be expected to be aware that work must sit within professional and legal frameworks, data security, EDI and sustainability among them, each in the subject's setting.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should be aware of the need to keep their work inside professional and legal frameworks, such as those on data security, EDI and sustainability, as they bear on MSOR.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be aware that your work has to fit professional and legal rules, including data security, equality, diversity and inclusion and sustainability, as they apply to mathematics.

statements.paraphrase: Graduates should be expected to keep to suitable ethical standards and be aware of the wider consequences of their work.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should keep to suitable ethical standards and stay alert to the wider consequences of what they do.

forBeneficiary.text: You should keep to sound ethical standards and think about the wider effects of your work.

statements.paraphrase: Graduates should be expected to start their own learning and to check and adjust their plans of work in the light of reflection and feedback.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should be able to initiate self-learning and monitor and adjust their own work plans in response to reflection and feedback.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to start learning on your own and to check and adjust your plans as you reflect and receive feedback.

statements.about: deeper professional skills and independence at master's level
statements.paraphrase: Master's-level students will have had deeper or broader experience of part of the professional skills listed, more experience of working independently and extra chances to devise new and creative approaches to non-standard problems.

forPractitioner.text: At master's level, graduates will have had deeper or broader experience of some of the 4.9 skills, more independent work and more chances to find creative approaches to non-standard problems; plan where these come.

forBeneficiary.text: At master's level you will have gone deeper or wider in some of these professional skills, worked more independently and had more chances to find new, creative ways into unusual problems.
